summary:
An astronaut has slept poorly for several nights, and their reaction time has slowed. A critical task is coming up, and medical support from Earth may be delayed. What should the crew do with the information they have?

We built Mission Pulse, a health-monitoring assistant that turns astronaut data into clear next steps. Four fictional crew profiles stream readings that change as each astronaut sleeps, exercises, or recovers. Mission Pulse compares those readings with personal baselines and connects changes across physical health, mood, and attention. Its AI summaries explain what changed, which readings support the explanation, and what the crew should check next.

Astronauts can point to discomfort on an interactive body map, ask the voice assistant COSO what to do next, or track exercise repetitions with a camera for you to have feedback on how to improve your workout sessions. By connecting early warning signs to practical actions, Mission Pulse helps crews decide when to keep monitoring and when to involve the Crew Medical Officer, even when Earth can’t answer right away.
details:
The problem we set out to solve

An astronaut has slept poorly for several nights, reports more distress than usual, and reacts more slowly on an attention test. Each change is easy to overlook on its own. Together, they raise a question the crew may need to answer before a critical task begins: is this a temporary fluctuation, or does it warrant a closer look? On a mission to Mars, a message to Earth could take up to about 22 minutes one way. The crew may need to make an initial decision while waiting for a reply.

How Mission Pulse works

Mission Pulse is a web-based health assistant built around a system that manages astronaut profiles. Each profile has a personal baseline, a health history, and a live feed that changes as the astronaut sleeps, works, exercises, or recovers. The dashboard brings together vital signs, sleep, emotional well-being, cognition, nutrition, activity, and environmental exposure. The crew can open any area to inspect the trend and see an explanation of what changed, what remains uncertain, and what to check next.

The crew can start with a reading, a symptom, or a conversation. The Body Map lets an astronaut select where they feel discomfort, see relevant measurements, and log what they noticed. The Measurement Guide explains what to prepare and record when using equipment documented by NASA, including sample collection kits and ultrasound. COSO, the voice assistant, can read back current figures, ask a follow-up question, and guide the astronaut toward an appropriate next step. When a report warrants escalation, the demo shows what can be done on board and whether the simulated handoff to Earth is queued or sent.

What makes the design different

The same change can mean different things in different contexts. A rising pulse during exercise and a sustained rise across resting measurements call for different questions. In Training Body, we use MediaPipe Pose Landmarker to track movement from a standard webcam. The demo can recognize supported patterns such as running, squats, push-ups, and overhead presses, then show estimated repetitions, steps, or movement range beside the video. Generated heart rate and breathing readings change with activity and recovery. Across the app, the explanations point back to the readings so the crew can inspect the basis for a recommendation.

We built Mission Pulse with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Canvas, and a Node.js server, and published the prototype on Replit. The OpenAI Responses API generates fictional telemetry and produces structured explanations from the available readings. The browser handles pose tracking and video display, while the server keeps the API key and handles AI requests.

Design decisions and intended impact

We built the workflow around three cases: a sustained change across several health indicators, a short-lived fluctuation followed by recovery, and a case with missing readings. Those cases helped us design for both missed deterioration and unnecessary escalation. We also considered crew workload, sensitive health information, and interruptions in communication. Observations stay associated with the selected astronaut, and initial emergency guidance is available locally in the demo.

Our goal is to help crews recognize meaningful changes earlier and preserve the reasoning behind decisions made on board. When the Crew Medical Officer or the team on Earth reviews a case, they can see what changed, what information was available at the time, and what the crew already did.
